verses.translation_literal: Praise Yah! Praise the name of YHWH! Praise, servants of YHWH,
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelujah! Let the praise begin. Lift up the name of the LORD, lift it high. Praise him, you who serve him, you who belong to the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a triple command: three imperatives of the same verb, הַלְלוּ, piled up like a crowd taking up the call. Hallelu-yah is not a single word of liturgy here but two words, 'praise' plus the short divine name Yah, and the second 'praise' is another beat in the drumroll. Say it the way a Levite choirmaster would call a congregation into the courts.

The KJV smooths this into 'Praise ye the Lord', flattening YHWH into a title and supplying 'him' (in italics in the KJV) after the third imperative, where the Hebrew has no object: the verb stands bare, and the servants are addressed directly. The Hebrew calls the addressees עַבְדֵי יְהוָה, 'servants of YHWH', a title of honour for those who work in his service. BBE rearranges the word order and loses the rising triple. Radak notes this psalm and Psalm 113 swap the order of 'praise the servants' and 'praise the name'. Here the name comes first, so the servants are named only at the end, where the next verse picks them up.

philological_notes.note: 'Praise Yah', the imperative of הלל followed by the short form of the divine name. The root is the source of the English 'hallelujah'. Here the phrase opens the psalm and is also repeated as a call in verse 3.
The 'name' stands for YHWH's revealed character and presence. Malbim distinguishes the name (his known, steady governance) from his 'remembrance' in verse 13.

verses.translation_literal: who stand in the house of YHWH, in the courts of the house of our God.
verses.translation_dramatic: You who stand within the house of the LORD, who wait in the courts of the house of our God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The servants are defined by where they stand. 'Standing' (עמד) is the ancient word for being on duty before a master or a deity, so these are priests and Levites in service, and, in Radak's reading, the ordinary Israelites in the outer courts too. The two phrases may mark two circles: the house itself, where only priests entered, and the courts, where the rest of the people prayed. Malbim takes it that way, with an inner and an outer ring of worshippers.

The KJV 'Ye that stand' is accurate; BBE's 'You who are in the house' loses the posture, and its 'open spaces' for חַצְרוֹת is an odd choice. The word means the enclosed open courtyards around a sanctuary. Play the line standing, hands at the sides, upright like an attendant at the door of a king.

philological_notes.note: 'Who are standing', with the relative שֶׁ- (a late and informal relative particle) and a participle. In temple language to stand is to serve; the same verb is used of Levites on duty.
Enclosed courtyards of the sanctuary, the outer area where the people gathered, as opposed to the temple building itself.

verses.translation_literal: Praise Yah, for YHWH [is] good; sing to his name, for [it is] pleasant.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise Yah, for the LORD is good. Sing to his name; sing, for it is sweet.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two reasons, two imperatives, mirrored: praise because he is good; sing because the singing is pleasant. The subject of 'pleasant' is ambiguous, and both readings have supporters. It may be the name, or the act of singing itself. Ibn Ezra takes it as a description of the honoured name; Meiri reads it as a goodness so complete it is 'sweet'. Keep the ambiguity alive in delivery: a half-smile on the last word.

The KJV 'sing praises' for זַמְּרוּ is fine, but the verb זמר is specifically to make music, with an instrument, not simply to sing. This is a call to the temple orchestra as much as to the choir. 'Pleasant' (נָעִים) is the same word used of David as 'the sweet psalmist of Israel' (2 Sam 23:1), the word of lyre and melody.

philological_notes.note: To make music, to sing with instruments. A different verb from הלל, so the verse calls for both speech-praise and played song.
'Pleasant, sweet'. It can describe the name or the act of singing; Ibn Ezra reads it of the name.

verses.translation_literal: For Jacob Yah has chosen for himself, Israel for his treasured possession.
verses.translation_dramatic: For Jacob is the one the LORD chose, chose for himself; Israel is his own treasure, set apart.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the first reason for praise is given: election. The Hebrew puts the objects first, 'Jacob... Israel', so the emphasis falls on who was picked, not on the act. Jacob and Israel are parallel names for the people. The line has a possessive pair: לוֹ 'for himself' and לִסְגֻלָּתוֹ 'for his treasure'.

סְגֻלָּה is not 'peculiar', as the KJV has it. In 1611 'peculiar' meant 'one's very own', but today it suggests oddness. The word names a king's private hoard: valuables set aside from the treasury, as in 'the treasure of kings' (Eccl 2:8), which Metzudat Zion cites. The same word appears in Exodus 19:5. BBE's 'property' is flatter, with no sense of cherished wealth. Say it as someone describing a thing they keep in a locked box and look at often.

philological_notes.note: Private treasure, a ruler's personal store of precious things. Of Israel, it means a people held as the king's own, apart from ordinary property.
'Chose for himself': the dative לו marks the choice as made for his own purposes, not on a trial basis.

verses.translation_literal: For I, I know that YHWH [is] great, and our Lord [is] above all gods.
verses.translation_dramatic: I know it. I myself know it: the LORD is great, and our Lord stands above every god.
verses.directors_commentary:
A single voice breaks out of the choir. אֲנִי is an independent pronoun, used where the verb already says 'I', so this is emphatic: I, for my part, I know. The speaker is witnessing from experience, and the verse turns from the group to the individual before a catalogue of acts follows. Radak understands the 'I' as the psalmist who has seen the wonders; Malbim, as a Jew who needs no signs because daily nature is evidence enough.

The KJV 'above all gods' is right in sense, but the Hebrew מִכָּל־אֱלֹהִים is 'than all gods', a comparative: greater than every other power called divine. For the ancient audience, 'the gods' were real forces, storm-gods and sea-gods, with other nations' temples. The psalm does not argue that they do not exist; it says they are less. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'gods' as the heavenly host or angels who run the world on his orders. The word אֲדֹנֵינוּ, 'our lord', also sets him as master of a household: the one who holds our contract.

philological_notes.note: Emphatic 'I, I know': the pronoun is not needed grammatically. The speaker knows from experience, not report.
'More than all gods': comparative min. Radak and Ibn Ezra read 'gods' as heavenly powers and idols; Meiri as the host of heaven worshipped by the nations.

verses.translation_literal: All that YHWH desires he does, in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and all deeps.
verses.translation_dramatic: Whatever the LORD desires, he does: in the heavens, on the earth, in the seas, in every deep that lies below.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the proof of verse 5: no one stops him. The verb חָפֵץ is 'to delight in, to will', and the whole clause says his wish and his act are the same thing. The merism is vertical: heavens, earth, seas, deeps. This is the three-storey world of the ancient Near East: sky above, land in the middle, the waters below and around. Everything a Canaanite or Babylonian would assign to a different god (sky-god, earth-goddess, sea-god) is his territory.

תְּהוֹמוֹת, 'deeps', is plural of תְּהוֹם, the primeval ocean of Genesis 1:2, the chaos waters that Near Eastern myth made a monster. The KJV 'all deep places' reads it as geography. Here they are just a realm he rules. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'depth of waters'. The KJV also puts the verb in the past ('pleased... did he'), whereas the Hebrew perfect states a general truth; say it as an always-true present.

philological_notes.note: To delight in, to will. Here it describes his sovereign wish, which is always carried out.
The deeps, the primeval waters below the earth. Metzudat Zion glosses 'depth of the waters'.

verses.translation_literal: Bringing up risers from the end of the earth, lightnings for the rain he makes, bringing out wind from his storehouses.
verses.translation_dramatic: He draws the clouds up from the far rim of the earth; he strikes the lightning to herald the rain; he lets the wind out from the storehouses where he keeps it.
verses.directors_commentary:
From cosmic claim to a weather report. Three participles describe what an Israelite watching a storm roll in from the Mediterranean would see: clouds rising from the horizon, lightning, then wind. In Canaan this is Baal's work: Baal is the rider on the clouds, the lightning-spear, the giver of rain. Here every piece is YHWH's, the same polemic as Elijah's drought in 1 Kings 17.

נְשִׂאִים, from 'to lift', literally 'those lifted', so 'risers': clouds or mists (Radak, Metzudat Zion). The KJV 'vapours' is a physical term; the Hebrew picture is simpler. מִקְצֵה הָאָרֶץ, 'from the end of the earth', means where land meets sea on the horizon, which is where storms visibly begin (Radak: from the sea). 'Lightnings for the rain' is a small puzzle: they are for the rain, as a signal or accompaniment, and Radak marvels that fire and water coexist.

אוֹצְרוֹתָיו, 'his storehouses', pictures wind kept in a warehouse like grain, to be released on order. The KJV 'treasuries' is a bit grand. Rashi: מוֹצֵא means that he finds, locates, so the winds are somewhere he has put them. In Job 38:22 the snow and hail are stored the same way.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'those lifted': rising clouds or mists. Radak and Metzudat Zion say clouds; Meiri discusses the dry vapour that rises with the damp.
Storehouses for grain or treasure. Wind is pictured as stored goods, to be brought out as needed.

verses.translation_literal: Who struck the firstborn of Egypt, from humankind to animal.
verses.translation_dramatic: It was he who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, from the man to the beast.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone shifts from weather to history. The relative שֶׁ- again, with a verb of violence: הִכָּה, 'to strike', the verb used of the tenth plague. The point is that the same hand that arranges rain also strikes the heir of every house. The Egyptian firstborn were the family's future, legal heir and priestly successor; Pharaoh's own son counted as divine. Livestock were struck too, because in Egyptian religion animals were sacred.

The KJV 'both of man and beast' is a fine rendering of מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה, 'from human to animal', but the Hebrew is a range with endpoints, not a pair. The sense is complete reach. אָדָם is 'humankind' without regard for sex. BBE's 'first-fruits' for בְּכוֹרֵי is a mistake: the word is firstborn.

Radak says the psalmist names this plague alone because by it Israel went out.

philological_notes.note: Firstborn, the heirs. Radak says this plague is singled out because it led to the exodus.

verses.translation_literal: He sent signs and wonders in your midst, Egypt, on Pharaoh and on all his servants.
verses.translation_dramatic: He sent signs and wonders into your very heart, O Egypt: against Pharaoh, against every one of his servants.
verses.directors_commentary:
Suddenly the psalm speaks to Egypt itself: 'in your midst, O Egypt'. The poet turns and addresses the victim, a thundering second-person aimed across the centuries. Say it directly, as to someone in the room.

The suffix of בְּתוֹכֵכִי has an old feminine -ki, as if Egypt were a woman addressed. Rashi and Radak read it as a form of 'בתוכך'; Radak calls the extra yod a grace of style. The KJV 'tokens' for אֹתוֹת is archaic: 'signs'. מוֹפְתִים is 'wonders', portents which point beyond themselves. The two words appear together as a standard phrase for the plagues.

'Pharaoh and all his servants' means the court and administration, since in Egypt the king's officials were the state. Metzudat David notes the plagues did not reach Israel in their own land.

philological_notes.note: 'In your midst', with an old poetic feminine second-person suffix -כִי, addressing Egypt directly as 'you'. Rashi and Radak say it is the same as בתוכך.
'Signs and wonders', the fixed pair for the plagues. Radak says the pair covers the other plagues beyond the firstborn.

verses.translation_literal: Who struck nations many and killed kings mighty,
verses.translation_dramatic: It was he who struck down many nations, and put mighty kings to the sword.
verses.directors_commentary:
From Egypt to the conquest of Canaan, again with שֶׁהִכָּה, 'who struck', so the conquest is credited to him rather than to Israel's army. The adjectives follow the nouns in the Hebrew: nations many, kings mighty, and the sense is one of overpowering numbers and strength. Radak points out that Israel, just out of slavery, was small and the nations were many and strong, so it must have been YHWH's hand.

The Hebrew verb is two different words: הִכָּה, 'struck', and הָרַג, 'killed'. The KJV's 'smote' and 'slew' are accurate but archaic; today they sound like Bible-speak, whereas 'killed' is blunt. Keep the bluntness in performance. In the ancient world, defeating a king meant killing him: this is not abstract.

The word גּוֹיִם is 'nations' without any note of other-ness here, the peoples of the land.

philological_notes.note: Mighty, strong, numerous. From a root meaning bone, strength.

verses.translation_literal: Sihon king of the Amorite, and Og king of the Bashan, and all kingdoms of Canaan,
verses.translation_dramatic: Sihon, king of the Amorites; Og, king of Bashan; and every kingdom of Canaan.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two named kings are the first victories east of the Jordan (Num 21), and then 'all the kingdoms of Canaan' sweeps up the rest. Radak says these two are named because they were fought first and were strongest. Sihon ruled from Heshbon; Og ruled Bashan, the rich plateau famous for cattle and for giants. Naming defeated kings was an ancient way of listing conquests, like a victory stele.

The Hebrew has the preposition ל- on each name: לְסִיחוֹן, 'to / of Sihon'. This is the accusative marker used with a verb of killing, so 'killed Sihon' (Metzudat Zion compares 'killed Abner', 1 Sam 3). The KJV hides this by writing the names as plain apposition. The construction 'the Amorite' is a singular collective (Hebrew has 'the Amorite' where English wants 'the Amorites').

philological_notes.note: The ל- here marks the object of the verb, as in 'killed Abner'. Metzudat Zion cites 1 Sam 3 for the pattern.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave their land [as] an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.
verses.translation_dramatic: And their land he gave as an inheritance: an inheritance for Israel, his own people.
verses.directors_commentary:
The conquest ends with a gift. The verb is נָתַן, 'gave', not 'took', and the doubled word נַחֲלָה, 'inheritance', rings like a deed read twice. Land in the ancient world was inherited, passed from father to son and not to be sold outside the family; to call it נַחֲלָה is to say Israel holds it as a family holds an estate, from a grantor. Malbim says the gift fulfils the promise to the patriarchs.

The KJV 'heritage' is a fine older word for the same; BBE's 'even for a heritage' adds 'even', which the Hebrew does not. The repetition is deliberate: say it twice, the second time slower. Note also 'Israel his people': it returns to the 'chosen' of verse 4 and closes the arc from election to land.

philological_notes.note: Inherited family estate: land held by right of descent. The doubling emphasizes the gift.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, your name [is] for ever; YHWH, your remembrance [is] to generation and generation.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD — your name stands, and it will stand when every other name has been spoken and lost. O LORD — you will be remembered, and the remembering will be handed down, father to son, generation to generation, without a gap.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has no verb. Two bare nouns with the divine name set in front of each, 'YHWH, your name — for ever; YHWH, your remembrance — to generation and generation', and the missing verb makes it sound like a creed chanted by a crowd. Both halves are an echo of Exodus 3:15, where God gives Moses the name and says 'this is my name for ever and this is my remembrance (zikhri) to generation and generation'. The singers are quoting the burning bush back to God. Play it as a line they know by heart.

The KJV adds 'endureth' and 'throughout all' and turns 'remembrance' into 'memorial', which is a fair guess but makes the line a statement about durability instead of a recital. In the ancient world a name was a person's presence and reputation; a god whose name was forgotten was a dead god, and the gods of the nations, as the next verses say, are things made of metal. The word 'olam is 'for ever' only in the sense of 'to the farthest horizon you can see': the same word, set against 'generation and generation', gives time as a chain of people passing something on.

philological_notes.note: 'Your remembrance': what is said and recalled about someone, so the name in the mouth of later generations. It is the word of Exodus 3:15, where it stands in parallel with 'my name' just as here. KJV 'memorial' is old English for the same thing.
Literally 'to generation and generation', the doubled noun being the Hebrew way of saying 'every generation'. The repetition is the point: a chain, not a span.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH will judge his people, and over his servants he will relent.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD himself will take up the case of his people and give them justice; and when he looks on his servants, his heart will turn, and the anger he held against them will ease.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb yadin is 'he will judge', but the judging here means taking up a case on behalf of the people and putting it right, the way a king sits in the gate and rules for the wronged side. It is a verdict in Israel's favour, not a threat. The KJV 'judge' leaves a modern reader thinking of a courtroom at which Israel is on trial. Meiri takes it as 'he will take their judgement and their vengeance from the nations'.

The second half is a quotation of Deuteronomy 32:36, the Song of Moses, and the verb yitnecham is the one the KJV renders 'repent himself', a phrase that sounds like admitting a fault. It means to feel sorrow over something and so change course, as in Exodus 32:14. God's anger, not his judgement, is what turns. Malbim reads it as God setting aside the laws of nature for a moment on behalf of his people, as when he told the sun to stand still. Here it is the 'because' (ki) which links the verse to what came before: his name lasts because he keeps acting for his people.

philological_notes.note: 'To judge', in the sense of arguing a cause or giving someone justice. With 'his people' as object it means vindicate; compare Deuteronomy 32:36, from which the line is taken.

Hithpael of nacham: to be sorry, to relent, sometimes 'to console oneself'. Said of God it describes a change of intention in response to his people's condition, not an admission of error; Meiri says such phrases are used of God 'by way of figure'.

verses.translation_literal: The idols of the nations [are] silver and gold, the work of the hands of man.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the gods of the nations — look at them. Silver. Gold. Metal, bought by weight and shaped at a bench: the work of a man's hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn from the God of Israel to the gods of the nations is abrupt, and it is meant to feel like a slap. These are not called 'gods' (elohim) at all; they are 'atzabbim, 'idols', a word Ibn Ezra hears as 'sorrows', since the root atsav means pain and toil, so that the idol is a thing that earns its maker nothing but trouble. A hearer would catch the pun on 'itstsavon (toil).

The KJV 'heathen' is the wrong word: goyim just means 'nations', every people other than Israel, and the verse is about their objects of worship, not their character. 'Silver and gold' is not praise. The metals are the most valuable the ancient world had, and the point is that the most precious god is still raw material that a craftsman cast, poured and polished. Isaiah 44 and the Babylonian rituals for 'opening the mouth' of a statue show the ritual world behind it: a statue was made divine by ceremony, and the Psalm says the ceremony is made by the same hands. The line is repeated almost word for word in Psalm 115:4.

philological_notes.note: 'Idols of'. Ibn Ezra takes the word as one of contempt, tied to the root 'to hurt, to grieve': things which bring only grief.
'The work of the hands of man'. The maker is man, who is himself made by God, so Ibn Ezra says the maker is more honourable than what he makes.

verses.translation_literal: A mouth [belongs] to them, and they do not speak; eyes [belong] to them, and they do not see.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have a mouth, carved with care — and it never speaks. They have eyes, bright and wide — and nothing is seen.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew puts the thing first and says 'mouth — to them' and then 'and not they speak': the contrast comes in a flat, mocking beat. The first two limbs are mouth and eye, and Ibn Ezra notes that these are the most honoured of the senses, speech being the gift of the soul that lifts man over the animals. The KJV 'They have mouths... eyes have they' is accurate but turns the tight pairs into a chatty sentence, and the singular 'mouth' (peh) is lost: the statue has one carved mouth, a thing made to look like a mouth.

This is polemic against the cult image of the nations. In Mesopotamia and Egypt the statue was fed, dressed and carried out in procession, and its eyes and mouth were ritually 'opened'. The Psalm answers the ritual with a plain inventory: every part is there, and none works. Verses 15-18 repeat Psalm 115:4-8, and Radak and Meiri refer the reader back there.

philological_notes.note: 'They speak'. The Piel imperfect describes habitual speech, so 'they never speak'. The same root gives 'word', and the god who speaks is set against gods who do not.

verses.translation_literal: Ears [belong] to them, and they do not give ear; also, there is no breath in their mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have ears, shaped and set on either side — and no sound ever reaches them. Lean close to the mouth, as you would to a sleeper to learn whether he lives: nothing stirs. There is no breath there at all.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse runs the same test as verses 15–16 on one more organ, then goes further. Ears that do not give ear: the Hebrew plays on the noun 'oznayim ('ears') and the verb ya'azinu ('they give ear'), both from the same root, so the idol's ears are named and then denied their one function. Keep the echo audible.

The last clause is the sharpest. 'Also' (af) marks a step beyond the last: it is not only that they cannot hear or speak, there is no breath in the mouth. The double negation 'ein-yesh' ('there is not there-is') is emphatic, a flat denial of existence. To the ancient audience breath (ruach) was the sign of a living creature, so a statue without it is not merely inert but dead matter. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as the idol lacking even the breath an animal has; Radak reads it as lacking even the breath that goes out through the mouth from the heart. The Targum makes it explicit with 'the breath of life'. Genesis 2:7 is a nearby idea, not the same word: there God breathes into Adam's nostrils the neshamah of life ('breath of life'), a near-synonym of ruach, so the contrast between a living human and a made image is easy to hear. The KJV 'neither is there any breath' turns the particle af into a connective 'neither', softening the climax into one more item on the list; 'indeed, not even breath' is closer.

philological_notes.note: A verb made from the noun 'ear' (ozen): 'to give ear, to listen'. The Hebrew names the ears and then uses their own root for the act they fail to perform.

Here the particle 'also, indeed, moreover', marking a step beyond the previous point. The same consonants spell 'nose', and YLT reads 'Nose' here. Rashi comments on the vocalisation, noting pataḥ here against qamets in Psalm 115:6, where 'af is the nose.

Breath, wind, spirit. In the mouth it is the breath of life: Rashi and Metzudat David say the idol lacks even the breath an animal has; Radak, the breath that passes out through the mouth from the heart.

verses.translation_literal: Like them will be those who make them, every one who is trusting in them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let those who made them become like them — mute, blind, deaf, breathless; and everyone who has trusted in them, the same.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has no 'so is' and no 'that': it is two phrases laid side by side, 'like them will be their makers — every one trusting in them'. The verb yihyu is imperfect, and commentators split on whether it is a prediction or a curse. Radak and Metzudat David hear a wish (let them become like them), Radak also allows a future event; Malbim takes it as a statement of cause and effect, that those who rely on such things can receive no more than the things have to give. The KJV picks the prediction, 'are like unto them'. Either way the sting is the same: the one who gives his trust to something that cannot act becomes unable to act himself.

It is also a point about what you are worshipping. The maker pours the hours of his life into an object, and the object is the one with nothing to give back. The line is identical to Psalm 115:8. The sentence turns on the word 'trusting' (boteach), the same word used elsewhere for trust in a fortress or a king, so it names a real dependence, not a religious feeling.

philological_notes.note: A poetic form of 'like them', with the long suffix. The extra syllable makes the phrase heavy, the way a verdict is.
'Trusting', 'feeling secure'. Used of leaning your weight on something. Metzudat David reads the whole verse as a curse.

verses.translation_literal: House of Israel, bless YHWH; house of Aaron, bless YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: House of Israel — all of you, the whole gathered people — bless the LORD! And you, house of Aaron, you who stand nearest the altar, bless the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
After the cold inventory of the idols, the psalm turns to the living, and the verbs become commands. 'Bless' (barakh) is the same word that closes the psalm in verse 21 and is the key to the ending: the dead gods give nothing, so the people give blessing to the God who does. Radak reads it as thanks for rescue from the worshippers of images; Metzudat David, for being set apart from the idolaters.

The summons works through a roll call. The same calls appear in Psalm 115:9–11 and 118:2–4, but there in three parts: Israel, the house of Aaron, those who fear YHWH. Psalm 135 adds a fourth group, the house of Levi, in the next verse. Ibn Ezra describes the order here: first the whole people (the house of Israel), then the priests, 'the most honored of the honored', the house of Aaron, then the whole tribe (Levi), and last the widest circle, all who fear YHWH. Direct it as a procession through ranks, each group answering in turn; the house of Aaron are the priests, who serve before YHWH (Radak), and Meiri takes the pair as general then particular.

The KJV's 'Bless the Lord, O house of Israel' moves the vocative after the verb and so loses the Hebrew opening, in which each group is named first, like a name called across a courtyard. The Hebrew order puts 'house of Israel' first, then the command.

philological_notes.note: 'House of' stands for a household or lineage: here the whole descendants of Israel and the priestly line of Aaron. Used as the address of a roll call.

Imperative plural, 'bless!'. The verb is the one used when people bless God, meaning to speak of him with gratitude and acknowledge him as the source of good, in contrast to the idols, who give nothing.

verses.translation_literal: House of the Levi, bless YHWH; fearers of YHWH, bless YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: House of Levi — bless the LORD! And you who stand in awe of the LORD — you, too — bless the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
The list reaches its widest ring. The Levites served the sanctuary with song and instruments (Radak: 'with mouth and instrument'), and the first half of the verse is for them. The second half is open: 'fearers of YHWH' is not a tribe, and it names no family. Ancient commentators disagree about who they are. Rashi, citing a midrash, says converts to the faith; Metzudat David, the pious of the nations; Radak, either the scholars of Israel who study in the temple or those from other peoples who came to pray there. Keep the ambiguity: the actor should say the line as a door left open.

The KJV 'ye that fear the Lord' is fine, but 'fear' has to be heard as reverence, not terror (yare' is the word for the awe a person feels before someone far greater). The phrase 'house of the Levi' has the definite article on the name, 'the Levi', which is the form that treats Levi as a class, a role in the cult, and not as a single ancestor.

philological_notes.note: 'Fearers of YHWH', a title for those who revere him, the awe and respect owed to a king. Whether it means born Israelites, converts or the pious of the nations is disputed by the commentators.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [be] YHWH from Zion, dwelling Jerusalem. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be the LORD — from Zion, from the hill itself, where he dwells in Jerusalem! Hallelujah. Praise the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends where it should, in the city. The idols were carried, set up, and dumb; YHWH is blessed 'from Zion', where he dwells. The preposition min ('from') has two plausible senses. Radak takes it as the source of instruction and glory: there the divine glory dwells and from there teaching goes out to all who fear him. Metzudat David takes it as the light of the Presence shining from Zion. Malbim hears blessing rising from Zion and descending to the people according to their deeds. Play it as direction: the praise starts in Jerusalem and spreads outward, so the actors turn toward the Temple.

The participle 'dwelling' (shokhen) stands bare before 'Jerusalem', with no preposition and no 'who'; the Hebrew simply says 'dwelling Jerusalem'. The KJV keeps 'out of Zion' but supplies 'at' before Jerusalem and a relative 'which', which smooths what is a plain apposition. The verb shakhan is also the root of shekhinah, the 'presence' the Targum names when it says 'whose Presence dwells in Jerusalem'. Against an idol that has a mouth but no breath, this is a God present in a city, at an address.

The last word is one word in Hebrew: 'halelu-yah', 'praise Yah!', plural imperative, the short form of the divine name. The KJV's 'Praise ye the Lord' turns it into an English phrase and loses that the name Yah is inside the command.

philological_notes.note: 'From Zion', with min as source. Radak understands it as the place from which the Presence shines and instruction goes out; Malbim, as the place from which blessing rises and returns to the people.
Participle of 'to dwell, to settle, to tabernacle'. It stands in apposition to YHWH; the Targum renders it with 'whose Presence (shekhinta) dwells', and the root underlies the later term shekhinah.
'Praise Yah': plural imperative of halal plus Yah, the short form of the divine name. It closes the psalm as it opened it in verse 1.
